name: EMS suit / electrical muscle stimulation
lead: Electrical muscle stimulation (EMS, also called NMES or electromyostimulation) uses electrical impulses delivered through skin electrodes to make muscles contract, and is used in rehabilitation, athletic training and consumer fitness [1]. Whole-body EMS suits apply electrodes across many muscle groups at once and are sold commercially for fitness.

Small randomized trials of whole-body EMS in healthy adults exist [2][3], and a Danish case report describes rhabdomyolysis after a whole-body session [4]. No trial found here measures muscle appearance as an outcome.
infobox: FDA divides EMS devices into OTC (toning) and prescription (therapeutic) classes [1]
Small trials in healthy adults; low-certainty in clinical populations

paras: Luigi Galvani provided early evidence in 1761 that electric current can activate muscle, and in the 1960s Soviet sports scientists used EMS with elite athletes and reported large force gains; Western replication in the 1970s gave conflicting results [1].

EMS is used to limit muscle atrophy during inactivity or injury, and as a training adjunct in healthy people [1]. A Cochrane review cited by Wikipedia found quadriceps strength gains in people with advanced disease but graded the evidence low certainty [1]. Reviews also found results depend on the stimulation protocol [1]. Wikipedia describes calorie burn from EMS as marginal and notes the FDA does not certify devices that claim weight reduction [1].

Listed contraindications include pacemakers, fractures, burns, skin lesions and deep vein thrombosis, and adverse effects include skin irritation and burns [1]. The FTC has challenged consumer EMS devices with unsubstantiated claims [1]. A 2023 case report describes rhabdomyolysis in a young woman after whole-body electromyostimulation training [4].

A randomized trial with 64 healthy men examined the efficacy and safety of whole-body EMS using a graded exercise test [2]. A randomized controlled trial in 24 young women examined a whole-body EMS suit's effects on strength and balance [3]. Results details were not available in the abstract text reviewed. No trials measuring muscle size or appearance were found.

card.summary: Electrodes that make muscles contract; real in rehab, small trials in fitness, nothing on looks, with rare serious harms reported.
card.note: Rhabdomyolysis case reported after whole-body sessions; contraindicated with pacemakers.

quick.overview:
EMS uses electrical pulses to trigger muscle contractions, and whole-body suits do this across many muscles during a workout. It is established in rehabilitation and marketed for fitness.

Small trials in healthy adults exist, but none found here measure muscle appearance.
quick.mechanism: Pulses through skin electrodes depolarize motor nerves and make muscle fibers contract, and are said to recruit fast-twitch fibers [1].
quick.risks: Skin irritation and burns are listed adverse effects, pacemakers and several conditions are contraindications, and a case of rhabdomyolysis after whole-body EMS has been reported.
